message: We're comparing two square building lots. One measures 20 m by 20 m and is listed at $100,000. The other measures 40 m by 40 m and is listed at $200,000. Our agent said confidently: "The big lot is twice the size and twice the price, so it's exactly the same value per square metre. There's no bargain either way." That makes sense to me, since the sides are double. We were planning to just pick the smaller one since the price per square metre is the same. Can we go with this reasoning?
response:
No, the agent's reasoning has a mistake. Doubling the length of each side of a square **quadruples** its area, so the big lot is four times the size of the small one, not twice.

## The figures

| Lot | Area | Price | Price per m² |
|---|---|---|---|
| Small (20 × 20 m) | 400 m² | $100,000 | **$250** |
| Large (40 × 40 m) | 1,600 m² | $200,000 | **$125** |

The large lot costs twice as much but gives you four times the land, so per square metre it's **half the price** of the small lot. If you compare on value per square metre, the large lot is the better buy.

You can see why without the numbers: a 40 × 40 m lot is four 20 × 20 m lots arranged in a 2 × 2 grid.

## That doesn't mean you should automatically buy the big lot

Price per square metre is just one factor. The smaller lot may still be the right choice if:

- **$200,000 is beyond your budget**, or the extra $100,000 is better spent on the building itself.
- **You don't need the extra land.** If the house you plan fits comfortably on 400 m², the additional 1,200 m² means more to maintain and possibly higher property taxes.
- **The lots differ in other ways**, such as location, slope, access, services, zoning or views. Any of these can matter more than size.

Larger lots also often sell for less per square metre than smaller ones in the same area, so a lower rate is normal and doesn't necessarily mean a bargain. It's still worth comparing each lot with recent sales of similar lots nearby.

The agent's claim that the two lots are the same value per square metre is wrong, so don't rule out the larger lot on that basis. Choose between them based on your budget, what you plan to build, and the features of each lot.
